pr_title: nvs: add a cycle counter for flash devices without erase functions
pr_body:
Devices that fall under Flash API with no-erase functionality have to emulate the operation by writing pre-defined value to erased area This takes a toll on memory endurance and needlessly occupies CPU and bus/memory.

Introduce a new mechanism for the NVS file system to handle empty sector or ATE by adding a cycle counter that is incremented each time a sector is erased

All valid ATEs in a sector must have the same cycle counter as the cycle counter that is stored in the "empty ATE"

The sector organization should look like this at anytime :

```
___________________________________________________________________
|            |              |             |           |           |
|... DATA ...| GC_DONE ATE  | ... ATEs ...| Empty ATE | Close ATE |
|____________|______________|_____________|___________|___________|

```
Empty ATE is the one holding the leading cycle counter for a sector. When closing a sector, the cycle counter in the close ATE should have the same value as the cycle counter in the empty ATE and all unused ATEs in that sector should be written with a garbage ATE

A sector can have multiple status :
Open sector : empty_ate.cycle_cnt == close_ate.cycle_cnt + 1 Closed sector : empty_ate.cycle_cnt == close_ate.cycle_cnt Never used Sector : Empty ATE or Close ATE invalid

Each time a sector is garbage collected and then erased, the cycle counter for that sector is increased to make all the ATEs in that sector invalid.

Fixes #69383 

This PR depends on the new common access interface that should define a way to access device characteristics like erasable/overwrite abilities :
https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/67687

In order to have a system failure when the garbage writing fails we need the following conditions :
1- Writing garbage ATE fails without reporting any error
2- In the next 255 cycles of writes of all sectors (meaning writing the whole sectors all over again 255 times), this ATE location will never be used by any ATE or data (always stays untouched)
3- In the next 255 cycles of writes of all sectors (meaning writing the whole sectors all over again 255 times), writing the garbage fails all the time for this location
4- When the garbage write fails, some how the CRC for that ATE is still valid
5- In the 256th cycle, we are going to write an ATE to this location and not a data

If we suppose that for a certain bit of a flash memory a failure could happen in 1/10000 cycles you can already see that this could almost never happen even in a million year

So here is a rational analysis if you still don't see the problem :
- gc_done has a variable position withing a sector. When trying to validate an ATE from a sector different than the current open sector we will need to search for the gc_done ATE in that sector to get the counter of that sector
- gc_done should always be a valid ATE within a sector and must carry the counter of that sector, it cannot hold the counter of an old erased sector, otherwise it will be considered as an invalid ATE in the current sector.
- If we use gc_done to store the counter that will determine if the current sector is valid or not then we will add more complexity to the recover : what happens if we fail to write the gc_done ATE ? Is it a garbage collection that didn't finish or is it the erase operation that failed ?

To be fair, I think that looking for a different solution where we don't add any ATE is going to make the recovery much more complicated.

NVS does not really care if an erase is done or not, it needs to find out if a area is writeable, and this is identified by looking if the erase-value is written in a certain area. For a device without erase any location would be writeable, but to make an ate writable it should contain a counter value (as in increased every time sector 0 is put into use) different from the present counter value or be invalid (from crc calculation).

To find out from what location can be written in a sector the data in the closing ate can be used, if it is the erased-value the erased-value can be used to find where the data is the erased value. If it is a valid ate with a counter equal to the "previous" counter value nvs knows it is running on a non-erase device, if it is an invalid ate the sector is badly closed and nvs does not need to know where to write in the sector. If it is badly closed a trial could be made to correct it (which will succeed on non-erase devices).

@Laczen About your suggestion to not add any new ATE to the NVS filesystem here are my comments :
- NVS is a fast-forward filesystem where we only write each ATE location in a sector once to maintain the wear leveling feature.
- For the close ATE, we write it once the sector is closed and we move forward to the next one
- For devices that need an erase before any write is done, we should keep this and NVS already looks for the erase value to know which area is writable.
- For devices that do not support erase, we should differentiate between valid ATE and invalid ATE for a new sector by incrementing a cycle counter. This operation cannot be done for a new sector using the close ATE because we are going to add a second write to that ATE when closing the sector which is going to kill the wear leveling feature.
- Adding a new ATE should solve the issue while keeping the wear leveling feature.

Please elaborate on how do you thing it is possible to keep only the close ATE, using a cycle counter, while keeping only one write for each ATE at each sector cycle write

> Please elaborate on how do you thing it is possible to keep only the close ATE, using a cycle counter, while keeping only one write for each ATE at each sector cycle write

A sector will be "opened" by writing the first ATE with the new cycle counter, it will be closed when the closing ATE is written with the same cycle counter. As long as the first ATE has a cycle counter that is different from the closing ATE cycle counter the sector is open and all valid ATE's have the same cycle counter as the first ATE. To extend this method to backends with erase functionality a sector is "opened" when the closing ATE is writable (see further).

When using nvs on a no-erase backend it is not required to keep any badly written ATE, it is simpler to just overwrite them. Even on systems that do require erase it is possible to try and rewrite the bad ATE if the sector is writeable (the closing ATE is writeable) and advance if this write fails. Checking whether an ATE is writable could be done as:
1. Check if the closing ATE is 0xFF (this covers the backend with erase),
2. If 1. fails, check if the closing ATE is valid with a cycle counter equal to the previous (for a no-erase backend),
3. If 2. fails, try rewriting with the erase value, if this succeeds (and this will only happen on a no-erase backend), it becomes writable,
4. If 3. fails the ATE is not writeable and the sector is closed.

The usage of a cycle counter would allow speeding up the nvs startup routine as it is possible to quickly search for the open sector. It even allows delaying the erase to the first write of a ATE to a sector.

1- relying on the first ATE to get the cycle counter instead of a header ATE is very dangerous for many reasons :
- That ATE could be deleted by the user or become obsolete if a new ATE with the same ID is written in the next sectors.
What happens when we run the garbage collector of that sector ? should we still consider that first ATE valid ?
- If we change the garbage collector logic to take into account obsolete or deleted ATE if it is the first ATE, then I am afraid that it will generate more bugs in the garbage collector mechanism if for some reason it is interrupted.

2- Avoiding to have an additional ATE header could maybe save some memory space but it will make the NVS filesystem non scalable in the future. If we need in the future to add more features or if we need a flag to set for a certain sector, having a new header will make these evolutions easier (the close ATE should not be used as it is written only when closing the sector)

The code is not killing the devices that do not need erase. Devices that do not need an erase like mram/fram have write cycles that highly outperform the erase-write cycles of flash, they have as they claim practically unlimited endurance. All that is done by nvs is an extra write cycle to set it to the erase value. If for some reason there are devices that do not have the practically unlimited endurance and there is a limit that is to small to allow for the write cycle to set it to the erase value nvs should not be enabled on them. Nvs and the settings system using nvs do their atmost best to avoid any unnecessary write, if even in this case the lifetime expectancy of the device is too low these devices should not be used for any storage solution..

The problem is not when systems are using 100% of memory space, the problem is when a sector is used at 100%. This depends on the data being saved but I'm confident that this happens in quite a lot of uses. There should not be a "lets try and see if it breaks" approach.

There are many manufacturing processes and often MRAM/RRAM and endurance of such devices may vary from 10k to several million cycles, depending on many factors from manufacturing process to read/write currents and operational temperature.

Overwriting device twice also costs in cpu cycles and power and, contrary to issuing erase, requires addressing each write-block-size unit separately; even if writes on such devices are quicker there is still a lot between where write ends and where it comes from, and such infrastructure is all time occupied writing the data.

This is very much visible if such device is connected via SPI, where instead of issuing one page erase command, and waiting, you will have the bus occupied for entire operation of simulated erase; this means there are far less things in your device you may put to sleep or be ding other things.

> > The code is not killing the devices that do not need erase. Devices that do not need an erase like mram/fram have write cycles that highly outperform the erase-write cycles of flash, they have as they claim practically unlimited endurance.
> 
> It is not true, the endurance of xRAM type devices depend on a layer they are placed on. There are many manufacturing processes and often MRAM/RRAM and endurance of such devices may vary from 10k to several million cycles, depending on many factors from manufacturing process to read/write currents and operational temperature.

Any device that has an endurance of less than 100k should not be considered for data storage.

> This is very much visible if such device is connected via SPI, where instead of issuing one page erase command, and waiting, you will have the bus occupied for entire operation of simulated erase; this means there are far less things in your device you may put to sleep or be ding other things.

This problem does not appear in zephyr as SPI devices without erase are not supported.

Anyhow, there is no reason to create a different solution for devices without erase. NVS is already used on these devices and this leaves no option but to make the transition smooth. This also rules out any addition of extra ATE's.

> 
> Any device that has an endurance of less than 100k should not be considered for data storage.

I lack understanding how you define the data storage, but here: https://documents.westerndigital.com/content/dam/doc-library/en_us/assets/public/sandisk/product/internal-drives/extreme-m2-nvme-pcie-ssd/data-sheet-sandisk-extreme-m2-nvme.pdf you can get data sheet for WD SSD 500GB and it has an endurance of 300TBW for a 500GB disk; this means that the disk can be written 600 times over before it dies... this is endurance of 0.6k.

> This problem does not appear in zephyr as SPI devices without erase are not supported.

Yet, but that was not the point. I mean this can be observed on SPI because it is exposed,  you can just connect to lines to scope and see or observe how other devices can not use it at that time. SoC consists internally of busses interconnecting various components; yes they are faster but they are still multiplexed and have limited bandwidth.

> 
> Anyhow, there is no reason to create a different solution for devices without erase. NVS is already used on these devices and this leaves no option but to make the transition smooth. This also rules out any addition of extra ATE's.

I do not understand why, honestly.  @rghaddab, the author here, is not breaking the original path, he just ports the solution to new kind of a device, allowing user to use the same driver for both types of devices in a way that is more aligned with what the device offers.

> > Any device that has an endurance of less than 100k should not be considered for data storage.
> 
> I lack understanding how you define the data storage, but here: https://documents.westerndigital.com/content/dam/doc-library/en_us/assets/public/sandisk/product/internal-drives/extreme-m2-nvme-pcie-ssd/data-sheet-sandisk-extreme-m2-nvme.pdf you can get data sheet for WD SSD 500GB and it has an endurance of 300TBW for a 500GB disk; this means that the disk can be written 600 times over before it dies... this is endurance of 0.6k.
>

Such a remark adds nothing to the discussion. It is clear I am referring to data storage in the context of nvs. There is a clear difference between the requirements for program storage and data storage. And yes this WD SSD should not be considered for data storage in the nvs context (if one ever wanted to use nvs on a 500GB disk).

> I do not understand why, honestly. @rghaddab, the author here, is not breaking the original path, he just ports the solution to new kind of a device, allowing user to use the same driver for both types of devices in a way that is more aligned with what the device offers.

There are several problems with the porposed solution:
1. Adding a specific ATE and building a complete new way of handling ATE's illustrated by the +/-700 lines that are added to the nvs system makes it impossible to provide good support for zephyr users,
2. The addition of a specific ATE and handling of the ATE's using this specific ATE is untested,
3. Adding a specific ATE cannot be done to existing nvs systems, because there might be no place for it,
4. NVS systems live independently of zephyr firmware, which means that if the zephyr firmware is using a new method to work with devices (there are no new devices added by e.g. PR #71271) it should be ok to upgrade to the new method of working with nvs, but it should also be possible to downgrade and step back to the old way of working with these devices.

Is it impossible to remove the above problems, I don't think so, but the PR as proposed is not the way to do it.

I see several methods to provide a correct solution:
1. Adapt nvs by using a cycle counter in an ATE but without using an extra ATE, several ideas how to do that have been proposed. This will not be a walk in the park given that verification needs to be done for upgrade and downgrade of zephyr firmware,
2. Make a new version of nvs that works on both devices with erase and without erase using a cycle counter in the ATE's and uses an extra ATE (but avoids the split handling of devices with and without erase). This will also not be a walk in the park because a upgrade path should be provided,
3. Make a new storage solution that is not limited to devices with erase and improves on any other limitations that are imposed by nvs (e.g. the difficulty to create a offline system that can be uploaded). This would also have the difficulty of providing a upgrade path,

Other solutions were also possible, when these devices without erase would have gotten their own proper api nvs could have been split up in dedicated solutions for each device type, but the introduction of #71271 has ruled out this possibility as subsystems now have to question a device about its type instead of finding it out trough the used api.

> * Check if the closing ATE is 0xFF (this covers the backend with erase),
> * If 1. fails, check if the closing ATE is valid with a cycle counter equal to the previous (for a no-erase backend),

Close ATE could be also 0xFFFF for no-erase backends if it has never been used => we should get the flash capabilities first

> I see several methods to provide a correct solution:
> 
> 1. Adapt nvs by using a cycle counter in an ATE but without using an extra ATE, several ideas how to do that have been proposed. This will not be a walk in the park given that verification needs to be done for upgrade and downgrade of zephyr firmware,
Removing the extra ATE will lead to more corner cases to handle with the no-erase backend.
Here is an example :
* An empty sector is currently found when the close ATE is entirely 0xffff (actually == erase_value)
* Using the no-erase devices we rely on the cycle counter in two header ATEs to find an open ATE using the condition => close_ate.cycle_cnt + 1 == empty_ate.cycle_cnt
* If we remove the empty ATE, we should rely on the cycle cnt of the first ATE in that sector to find out if it is open or not.
* If a sector contains already some ATE => no problem
* But if it is a sector that has never been used and no ATE exists there, the cycle_cnt of the first ATE could be a random value => it could be the same cycle value as the close ATE and we consider it as closed while it is not.
* That leads to the question : what is considered an open sector ?
- For devices with erase function a sector is considered open if it follows a closed sector and the first ATE is 0xffff
- For devices with no-erase there is a need to determine that based on the cycle_cnt
  => If we rely on the first ATE => impossible as it could not exist
  => If we rely on the last sector's close_ate cycle_cnt => there is a problem when the flash device has never been used or when it is the first sector of a new flash cycle (close_ate counter is increased)
  
> 2. Make a new version of nvs that works on both devices with erase and without erase using a cycle counter in the ATE's and uses an extra ATE (but avoids the split handling of devices with and without erase). This will also not be a walk in the park because a upgrade path should be provided,
for devices with erase (needs the memory to be erased) a sector should be erased before a write could be done (old cycle counters will be erased as well) => there is no benefit for these devices to use an extra ATE or to use the cycle counter

> 3. Make a new storage solution that is not limited to devices with erase and improves on any other limitations that are imposed by nvs (e.g. the difficulty to create a offline system that can be uploaded). This would also have the difficulty of providing a upgrade path,

Making a new storage solution could be the best solution for this discussion as it is clear that you disagree on separating support of erase/non-erase devices

> > I see several methods to provide a correct solution:
> > 
> > 1. Adapt nvs by using a cycle counter in an ATE but without using an extra ATE, several ideas how to do that have been proposed. This will not be a walk in the park given that verification needs to be done for upgrade and downgrade of zephyr firmware,

> Removing the extra ATE will lead to more corner cases to handle with the no-erase backend.
> Here is an example :
> 
> * An empty sector is currently found when the close ATE is entirely 0xffff (actually == erase_value)
> * Using the no-erase devices we rely on the cycle counter in two header ATEs to find an open ATE using the condition => close_ate.cycle_cnt + 1 == empty_ate.cycle_cnt
> * If we remove the empty ATE, we should rely on the cycle cnt of the first ATE in that sector to find out if it is open or not.
> * If a sector contains already some ATE => no problem
> * But if it is a sector that has never been used and no ATE exists there, the cycle_cnt of the first ATE could be a random value => it could be the same cycle value as the close ATE and we consider it as closed while it is not.
> * That leads to the question : what is considered an open sector ?
> 
> * For devices with erase function a sector is considered open if it follows a closed sector and the first ATE is 0xffff
> * For devices with no-erase there is a need to determine that based on the cycle_cnt
>   => If we rely on the first ATE => impossible as it could not exist
>   => If we rely on the last sector's close_ate cycle_cnt => there is a problem when the flash device has never been used or when it is the first sector of a new flash cycle (close_ate counter is increased)
>

 A sector is open when the first ate in a sector (not the closing ate location) is valid (has a correct crc) and the closing ate location is writeable (either it is all 0xff or the cycle cnt of the closing ate location +1 is equal to the cycle cnt of the first ate). This writeable definition is valid for both devices with erase and without erase.

issue_context.title: NVS: add support for flash devices without erase function
issue_context.body:
## Introduction

This RFC proposes a new method of recognizing  erased ATEs without having to erase entire sectors to handle NVS reads/writes operations.
This methhod is based on adding what is called a "cycle counter" that is incremented, for a given sector, each time we want to delete all the ATEs in that sector.

### Problem description

NVS filesystem operations are based on the fact that all memory cells are erased and in a known state before doing a write operation.
Devices that fall under Flash API with no-erase functionality have to emulate the operation by writing pre-defined value to erased area This takes a toll on memory endurance and needlessly occupies CPU and bus/memory.

One of the biggest advantage of using NVS for these devices is its wear leveling capabilities, but the amount of write operations that are added in order to erase sectors is affecting the life time of memory cells.
For normal operations, comparing flash devices that have normal erase functions with flash devices that should do write operations to erase memory cells, we get almost double of the number of write operations for the latter. Which means half of the life time expectancy.

### Proposed change

The proposed change will add a "cycle counter" parameter for each ATE that defines if a given ATE is still valid (cycle_counter == sector_cycle_counter) or erased/non valid (cycle_counter != sector_cycle_counter).
The change is also retro-compatible as it keeps the old mechanism of recognizing the erased cells using erase_value.

## Detailed RFC

### Proposed change (Detailed)

The main purpose of the proposed changes is to get rid of erasing the sectors and all parts of the code that compares the memory cells to a know value (erase_value) for all the NVS filesystem operations.
It also introduce these changes only for devices that needs this kind of feature while keeping the same operations for all other devices.
Please note that this new proposed method of recognizing erased cells could work as well for all the types of flash devices (erasable and non erasable). But it is limited for the moment for only non erasable devices to limit any risk of breaking systems that run using the old method.

**Global changes :**
- To keep the "nvs_ate" structure size unchanged we use the member "part" which is unused and we replace it by the cycle_counter
struct nvs_ate {
	...
	uint8_t part; => uint8_t cycle_cnt;
	...
} __packed;

- for flash_parameters we introduce a new flag : no_erase which is only meaningful for non erasable devices and defines whether a flash device is non erasable
- two CONFIGs are added : 
config NVS_FLASH_HAS_NO_ERASE
config NVS_FLASH_HAS_ERASE

These configs defines whether or not the NVS filesystem needs to use old operation method, new operations or both of them.
CONFIG_NVS_FLASH_HAS_ERASE is by default y and is defined when the other config NVS_FLASH_HAS_NO_ERASE is not defined.

**nvs.c changes :**
A new special ATE is introduced called empty ATE.
This ATE is the one holding the leading cycle counter for a given sector.
When a sector is being erased the empty ATE cycle counter is increased to make all the other ATEs in that sector invalid
When a sector is closed the close ATE cycle counter will get the same cycle counter as the empty ATE

The sector ATEs organization should look like this at anytime :
```
    _____________________________________________________________________
    |             |              |              |           |           |
    |... DATA ... | GC_DONE ATE  | ... ATEs ... | Empty ATE | Close ATE |
    |_____________|______________|______________|___________|___________|
```

A sector can have multiple status :
- Open sector : empty_ate.cycle_cnt == close_ate.cycle_cnt + 1
- Closed sector : empty_ate.cycle_cnt == close_ate.cycle_cnt
- Never used Sector : Empty ATE or Close ATE invalid

In the proposed changes the startup function for non erasable devices is "nvs_startup_noerase"
This function has almost the same operations as the old nvs_startup function but for readability purpose I prefer to separate it in a separate function as there are some differences between operation for erasable and non erasable devices.

### Dependencies

These changes depends on this [PR](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/67687/) which should introduce the flag to reconize erasable and non erasable devices
comments:
Hi @rghaddab! We appreciate you submitting your first issue for our open-source project. 🌟

Even though I'm a bot, I can assure you that the whole community is genuinely grateful for your time and effort. 🤖💙

> @rghaddab, thank you for this RFC. It would be a nice enhancement of nvs could be used without the need for erasing.
> 
> As a first remark i would say the config naming is badly chosen, the `FLASH` should be removed and it should just be `NVS_ERASE` and `NVS_OVERWRITE`.

I will change the CONFIG names.

> 
> Before going through the PR, a question arises about the `empty_ate`, is this being written each time a valid ate is written ? Has it been evaluated that even the write of a `empty_ate` can fail?
Empty ATE is not written each time a valid ATE is written, otherwise it won't make sense for wear leveling feature.
Empty ATE is only written when erasing a sector or when it is the first time using a sector.
I made sure that each ATE address is written at most once for each sector write cycle.

Regarding the fail of empty_ate write, I also took that into account.
When an empty ATE write fails, it means that trying to erase the sector failed.
On the next startup we have two cases :
- the empty ATE was partially written => the empty ATE is invalid (wrong CRC) => we fix the empty ATE if the close ATE is valid (note that writing the close ATE doesn't happen at the same time as writing the empty ATE, so both ATE writes could not fail at the same time)
- the empty ATE write didn't happen at all => the empty ATE cycle counter still have the close ATE cycle counter => the sector is considered as closed. If we find a GC_DONE in the previous sector it means that a GC has finished and we can erase the sector by adding an empty ATE, otherwise we must start again the GC.

@rghaddab, regarding the `empty_ate`, what would happen to the nvs storage solution if the crc of the `empty_ate` would be bad for a different reason (not after an incomplete write) ?

The use of a Kconfig option also limits the use of multiple nvs storage solutions when devices with and without erase are used, how would this be handled ?

> @rghaddab, regarding the `empty_ate`, what would happen to the nvs storage solution if the crc of the `empty_ate` would be bad for a different reason (not after an incomplete write) ?

Whether it is after an incomplete write or for any other reason, at startup NVS always checks for close sector followed by an open one and an empty sector :
If the empty ATE is invalid we fix it at startup when the close ATE is valid :
```
			/* we have to check if the close_ate or
			 * the empty_ate is valid.
			 * If one of them is valid it means that
			 * something wrong happened and either
			 * the close_ate or empty_ate write failed
			 * Let's fix the wrong ATE
			 */
			if (nvs_close_ate_valid(fs, &close_ate)) {
				/* update ate_wra to point to the address
				 * of empty ATE
				 */
				fs->ate_wra = addr - ate_size;
				rc = nvs_fix_empty_ate(fs, close_ate.cycle_cnt);
				if (rc) {
					goto end;
				}
				break;
			}
```
Or if the next sector (the empty one) has invalid empty ATE, then we create a new one.

> 
> The use of a Kconfig option also limits the use of multiple nvs storage solutions when devices with and without erase are used, how would this be handled ?

The Kconfig options can be both enabled. In this case the NVS driver can handle both types of storage based on the flag that is found on flash_parameters :

```
#if defined(CONFIG_NVS_OVERWRITE) && defined(CONFIG_NVS_ERASE)
#define NVS_DEVICE_HAS_NO_ERASE(fs) ((fs)->flash_parameters->no_erase)
#else
#define NVS_DEVICE_HAS_NO_ERASE(fs) IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_NVS_OVERWRITE)
#endif
```
@rghaddab looks like this can be closed too?

I understand that this change has been provided here to make it possible to work while support for `no-erase` devices is not ready yet, but, once the 67687 settles and merges, the change here will have to be removed.
